opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing. I don't think "pure LLM focus" accurately describes what Meta is doing, and I'm not going to speak for every strategic decision the company makes. There are different groups with different missions, and that has always been the case.

What I can tell you is where I stand. LLMs are useful. They're going to be deployed everywhere, and companies like Meta absolutely need to be competitive in that space. Investing in data, infrastructure, and talent to build better products in the short term makes complete sense from a business perspective.

But I've said this many times and I'll keep saying it: scaling up LLMs is not going to get us to human-level intelligence. These systems manipulate language very fluently, but they don't understand the physical world. They don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason, and they can't plan in any deep sense. A four-year-old has taken in more data through vision than the largest LLM has seen in text, and that child understands intuitive physics, object permanence, cause and effect. We have no idea yet how to get machines to learn like that from text alone, and I don't think we ever will.

So my work, and the work of the people I collaborate with, is focused on the next paradigm: systems that learn world models from sensory input like video, architectures like JEPA that make predictions in abstract representation spaces rather than at the pixel or token level, and systems that can plan by optimizing toward objectives with guardrails built in. That's a longer-term research agenda. It's not going to show up in a product next quarter.

My advice to young researchers hasn't changed: if you're interested in human-level AI, don't work on LLMs. That's in the hands of large companies with huge resources. Work on what comes next.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing. I don't think of it as a catalyst so much as a symptom. The Scale deal, and the whole Superintelligence Labs reorganization around it, was the company deciding it wanted to be in the frontier LLM race at full intensity, with the talent and the data pipelines that race requires. Scale was the data piece of that. So the shift came first, and the acquisition was one of the things you do once you've made that decision.

Now, was that the right bet? I've been pretty public about where I stand. I think LLMs are useful, I think they'll generate enormous value, and I also think they are an off-ramp on the road to human-level intelligence. Scaling up next-token prediction with more human-annotated data gets you a system that is very good at manipulating language and very bad at understanding the physical world, at planning, at persistent memory, at reasoning in the sense that an animal reasons. A cat has better common sense than any of these models. You don't close that gap by buying more labeled data.

So when I was running FAIR, my priority was always to keep a space for the longer-horizon stuff, world models, JEPA-style architectures, self-supervised learning from video. And I'd say the honest tension inside any big company is that the product people, quite reasonably, want the thing that ships next quarter, and right now that thing is an LLM. The danger with a pure LLM focus isn't that the LLMs will fail, it's that you starve the research that's going to make them obsolete in five years, and then someone else does it.

That's really why I left to do it on my own. Not out of any bitterness, Meta was very generous to the research for a very long time. But if you believe, as I do, that the next big thing is not a bigger language model, at some point you have to go build it.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t necessarily draw that conclusion. An acquisition can strengthen the work on LLMs without implying that all the research should converge on LLMs. Those are two different things.

The question is what you mean by a “pure LLM focus.” If you mean improving products built around language models, that’s one thing. If you mean that scaling language models is the entire path to human-level intelligence, I don’t think that’s right. We still need systems that understand the physical world, have persistent memory, can reason, and can plan. So I would distinguish the immediate product priorities from the longer-term research direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether Meta’s research should focus on LLMs, but does not speculate that Mark may view Alex as a potential successor.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t interpret it that way. An acquisition can strengthen your ability to build and deploy AI systems without settling the scientific question of what those systems should be.

LLMs are useful, and there are good reasons to invest in them. But I don’t think scaling language models alone is a path to human-level intelligence. We need systems that understand the physical world, have persistent memory, and can reason and plan. So I would separate the business decision from the research direction. I wouldn’t take the acquisition itself as evidence of a shift toward a pure LLM focus.
